text: {"headline":"Provider 1000000014 bills 99215 at about three times the complexity-adjusted expectation, but the small set of returned charts supports the billed levels, so the pattern is unresolved.","leaning":"inconclusive","interpretation":"The elevated 99215 rate holds in every complexity tier, roughly double the all-provider share even among zero- and one-condition patients, and the low-complexity sample includes 99215s for routine-looking encounters such as follow-up visits (C0009183, C0010234), upper respiratory infection (C0009328) and UTI (C0009167), which is the pattern of concern. Against that, none of the 16 documented 99215 claims fell below the billed level (supported examples include C0009228 and C0010020), which on its face is consistent with genuinely complex visits. That support is weak for two reasons: records cover only about 2% of claims, and roughly a third of returned notes show a duplicate-text signal, plus some repeated times and a few moderate-plus data-reviewed notes with no lab or test line. Those signals raise the possibility of cloned or templated documentation rather than proof of it, and no audit trail was received to check how the notes were created. A reviewer should first request charts for the sampled low-complexity 99215 claims and the audit trail, then compare the duplicate-flagged notes for copied content against the actual encounter details."}
